titreEditorial: Mistral AI raises €3 billion at a €21 billion valuation in a round led by Samsung; the labor-law scholar Jean-Emmanuel Ray reminds employers that the AI Act requires them to inventory their high-risk AI systems and inform staff by the end of 2027, while BPCE stands up its AI Factory and Bercy renegotiates the French state's IT contracts; China targets 9,800 eflops of compute and Huawei launches its first stacked-circuit chip; Revolut completes the first AI-initiated payment in France
chapeau: Mistral AI signs the largest European AI raise, €3 billion led by Samsung, at the moment its strategy is being questioned. The same day, France sees AI move into production everywhere at once, in a bank, at Bercy, at Revolut, as the AI Act starts counting the months before its first obligations toward employees.

une.titre: Mistral AI raises €3 billion, valued at more than €21 billion, with Samsung taking a stake
une.texteHtml: The French startup announces its largest funding round, €3 billion (about $3.5 billion), in a round led by Samsung Electronics, report Le Monde and Bloomberg. The valuation tops €21 billion, a record for an AI company in Europe. The deal comes as several experts fault Mistral for leaving the race for frontier models to focus on data centers and industrial deployment. Its CEO Arthur Mensch rejects that charge, says the company keeps producing top-tier models and considers himself still undervalued, betting on the eventual win of open-weight models (which you can download and run yourself). Samsung's entry, a Korean manufacturer, alongside European investors, anchors a bet: build in Europe both the compute infrastructure and the uses, without depending on the American and Chinese giants.

items.titre: The AI Act will require employers to inventory their high-risk AI and inform staff by the end of 2027
items.texteHtml: In his column for Le Monde, the labor-law scholar Jean-Emmanuel Ray advises human resources departments not to wait: by the end of 2027, they will have to inventory and clarify the artificial intelligence systems used in their departments, then inform employees. He revisits the workplace side of the AI Act, the European regulation on AI, whose obligations are drawing closer. The message is to take the inventory now, before the deadline turns it into an emergency.

items.titre: BPCE wants its AI Factory operational before the end of 2026
items.texteHtml: The banking group BPCE will have an AI Factory (an internal unit tasked with industrializing AI uses) this year, overseen by Yves Tyrode, chief AI, digital and payments officer, reports ZDNet. Its mission is to simplify the spread of AI across the bank's various business lines, from the adviser to the back office. The announcement illustrates French banks moving from scattered experiments to a dedicated organization.

items.titre: Bercy asks ministries to renegotiate their IT contracts in the name of AI-driven savings
items.texteHtml: David Amiel, minister for the budget and the civil service, urges ministries to reopen the contracts signed with the French state's IT suppliers, reports Clubic. The argument: thanks to generative AI, these suppliers produce more in less time, and Bercy wants that saving to benefit public finances too. The move raises a question that reaches beyond the public sector, that of how productivity gains are shared between the client who pays and the supplier who automates.

items.titre: Astra billed up to $33 for a single prompt
items.texteHtml: GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI's new model presented as a step toward AGI (artificial general intelligence), costs up to $33 for a single query, and it is not the priciest option in OpenAI's catalog, reports Next.ink. Since its release, several users have found that it burns through their usage quotas at speed. The figure gives a sense of the real cost of frontier reasoning: a single question put to the best model can be worth the price of a whole monthly subscription. For an organization working out an inference budget (the cost of running a model once it is trained), the price gap between a routine model and Astra changes the equation before any talk of value produced.

items.titre: Anthropic walks away from buying Decart AI for $6 billion
items.texteHtml: Anthropic has decided not to acquire the AI startup Decart AI, an acquisition valued at around $6 billion, according to sources close to the matter cited by Bloomberg. The report rests on anonymous accounts and has not been officially confirmed by either company. The retreat comes in a sector where labs are multiplying tie-ups to capture teams and technology. It suggests that Anthropic prefers, at this stage, to preserve its cash rather than pay a steep premium to grow through acquisition.

items.titre: AI leaders now describe AGI as a moving target
items.texteHtml: Reaching the point where AI performs most tasks better than a human used to pass as a measurable milestone; the heads of the major labs now present it as a fuzzy goal, one whose definition slips away as you get closer, reports Bloomberg. The shift in vocabulary matters: as long as AGI stayed a quantifiable threshold, you could argue over a date; now an elastic notion, it mainly serves to keep the promise alive. For the professional reader, the lesson is to judge these systems on what they do today in a specific job, not on the horizon attributed to them.

items.titre: China targets 9,800 eflops of compute by 2030, with clusters of 100,000 cards
items.texteHtml: China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology published on Monday a five-year plan setting a target of 9,800 eflops of intelligent computing capacity by 2030, a fourfold increase, reports the South China Morning Post. The plan calls for deploying compute clusters holding 100,000 accelerators each and an investment of 3.8 trillion yuan, about $532 billion. The effort targets the infrastructure that underpins the country's AI ambitions, at a time when US restrictions limit its access to the most advanced chips. Beijing answers with volume and state planning where access to frontier components is closed to it. The announced sum, more than $500 billion over five years, exceeds what most states devote to all of their public research.

items.titre: Huawei launches the Kirin 9050 Pro, its first commercial stacked-circuit chip
items.texteHtml: Huawei unveiled on Monday in Guangzhou the Kirin 9050 Pro, described by Richard Yu Chengdong, head of its consumer business, as its most powerful Kirin chip to date, reports the South China Morning Post. The component introduces the LogicFolding architecture, which stacks logic circuits vertically to gain performance without relying on transistor miniaturization alone, out of reach for a China under sanctions. It makes real the Tau scaling law that Huawei had defended on paper the previous week. The stakes go beyond the smartphone, launched in a tri-fold version: proving that the country can design frontier components on its own despite the American block on equipment. A first mass-produced product still says nothing about large-scale reliability or manufacturing yields, two points where the case remains to be made.

items.titre: South Korea aims for third place in world AI and merges its power utilities to feed it
items.texteHtml: Seoul wants to rise to become the third major global player in artificial intelligence, behind the United States and China, through massive investment and reforms, reports Le Monde. The ambition runs into internal resistance, over both the future of the labor market and the energy needs the country struggles to meet. A sign of that tension, the government plans to combine five state-owned electricity companies to prepare for the power demand of data centers and chip plants, reports Nikkei Asia. The Korean case shows that the AI race is played out as much on reactors and high-voltage lines as on models. A country that wants to train and run giant AI must first produce the electricity that feeds them.

items.titre: An AI-discovered drug reportedly reverses aging markers
items.texteHtml: An experimental treatment for a lung disease, designed with the help of artificial intelligence, has shown promising signs of reversing biological markers of aging, according to the lab developing it, reports Bloomberg. The result comes from a study run by the maker itself, at an early stage, and needs confirmation by independent work before any conclusion. The interest lies in the method: a molecule whose therapeutic target was identified by models, in a field, the biology of aging, where trials remain long and uncertain. Caution is due on a company announcement, but it illustrates AI's growing place in drug discovery.

items.titre: The CNRS warns that generative AI threatens the integrity of scientific publishing
items.texteHtml: Faced with a surge of AI-boosted studies and serial retractions, the CNRS (France's national scientific research center) sounds the alarm over the risk of a collapse in the reliability of the world's scientific publications, reports Clubic. The French body announces measures to preserve research integrity and slow an editorial drift it deems hard to contain. The subject touches directly the companies and administrations that rely on the scientific literature to decide.
Revolut, working with Visa, says it has completed the first online payment decided and executed by an artificial intelligence in France, a test presented as a foretaste of click-free purchasing.

items.titre: Astra clears a set of captchas built to unmask machines
items.texteHtml: An OpenAI engineer claims that GPT-6 Astra passed all 48 levels of "I'm Not a Robot", the neal.fun game that piles on anti-robot challenges, a machine passing a test invented to spot it.

analyse.titre: The labor-law scholar Jean-Emmanuel Ray reminds every employer that the AI Act will require them to inventory their high-risk AI systems and inform staff by the end of 2027, on the day BPCE announces its AI Factory, Bercy renegotiates its contracts in the name of AI-driven savings, and Revolut launches in France the first payment decided by an AI on its own: the skill that gains value is steering the social entry of AI as much as its technical entry, writing down for each system who it concerns and whether those people have been told, and taking the matter to the works council before the law sets the timetable
analyse.these: Jean-Emmanuel Ray warns in Le Monde: by the end of 2027, every employer will have to inventory the high-risk artificial intelligence systems used in their departments and inform staff about them. The deadline looks distant. It is not. The same day, BPCE announces an AI Factory operational before the end of 2026 to spread AI across all its business lines, Bercy asks ministries to renegotiate their IT contracts on the grounds that AI makes suppliers more productive, and Revolut completes in France the first payment launched by an AI on its own. AI is leaving the lab for production, department after department, often faster than management measures. The AI Act adds an obligation few anticipate: informing the people subject to these systems. Not only classifying them, documenting them, securing them. Telling employees that a machine screens their internal applications, scores their files, directs their tasks. That obligation shifts the introduction of AI from technical ground to social dialogue. A deployment once settled between a management team and a supplier becomes a matter for the works council. The skill that gains value in a French organization is steering the social entry of AI as much as its technical entry. Take each AI system already in use in a workflow. Write down who it concerns, which decision it affects for those people, and whether they have been told. Bring the subject to the works council before the law forces you to, while you still hold the choice of timing and framing. An empty table does not signal compliance postponed. It signals a blind spot that grows with every tool added. Between the moment the tool works and the moment the law requires you to explain it, a window remains. Trust is won or lost there. An employee accepts an AI that was introduced to them; they distrust the one they discover. The end of 2027 sets a legal deadline. The mood of a team is settled well before. The Masteria editorial team.
